posts.content:
We removed spending budgets in Q4 and it barely had any effect on our cash burn. 

Before PostHog raised our Series E I ran a model to project what our cash position would be until the end of 2028. This was in May 2025 and when we closed our July '26 books we were $200k lower than the number we predicted, about ~1% lower. (We're basically running this thing like Enron, I know). 

Now usually this is not something to shout about, but in Q4 '25 we made a big change where we basically removed spending budgets and gave everybody in the company a $5k a month budget on a company card and told them to "spend money in the best interests of PostHog" 

The obvious concern here was people would go crazy, but they haven't. They've treated this responsibly and people are now able to focus more on building rather than admin around spending. 

Trust is an incredibly strong motivator in a strong team.

That's enough seriousness for now, more memes tomorrow.

postedAt.postedAgoText: 1 week ago • Edited • Visible to anyone on or off LinkedIn

posts.content:
in the, just over 2.5 years I have been at PostHog, revenue has grown 15x. the Ops team (people & ops(3), talent(6), legal(1), finance(2), compliance(same 1 as legal)) has only grown 6x, and NEWSFLASH, we don't need to grow it that much going forward.

we've grown a lot in my time here but we've managed to keep a pretty lean team to fuel that growth. 

here's what those people actually did:
→ onboarded 200+ new joiners across ~29 countries
→ moved recruiting from 100% inbound to inbound + outbound
→ brought accounting in-house 
→ ripped out the old ERP for an AI-native one (Campfire)
→ built our own ops platform - this is so sick btw
→ held external legal fees FLAT in absolute terms through 15x revenue
→ took employee satisfaction from 83% to 98% (it was 100% one quarter) 🐐 

that's really only scratching the surface

but the honest version isn't "we did more with less". we did a genuinely different job with more people. We could have got by with slightly less, for sure. 

the 6x didn't go on more hands to process the same tickets. it went on people who could delete the tickets - build the platform, own the ledger, run outbound sourcing.
hiring ops people to automate ops work looks like the wrong trade on a headcount plan. however, it's the only one that stops us ballooning headcount from here. 


ps - the 83% → 98% is just from me making excellent contributions in the #dad-jokes slack channel

Fraser Hopper has done what most finance leaders only talk about: scale PostHog's finance function without increasing headcount.

Fraser uses Abacum to run FP&A for the whole finance function there, connecting ERP data to HR headcount data so the team can model hiring, spend, and revenue scenarios without a week of manual work in between.

He's been specific with us about why that matters. Real-time data changes what a finance team can actually act on, and without the ability to tag that data with AI, it wouldn't arrive fast enough to change a decision before it's already made.

And that precision pays off. 

PostHog's close went from 20-25 days down to under 10, while the team stayed lean instead of growing headcount to match the business. 

That combination is rare, and it's exactly the bar we want our customers holding us to.

That's the standard he's bringing to Abacum's advisory board and I couldn't be more excited to have him join!

repost.content:
Fraser Hopper cut 5-6 days off PostHog's monthly close in his first months on Campfire through tremendous growth.

When I first met Fraser, their teams revenue recognition was living entirely outside their accounting system, and with multi-entity consolidation on QuickBooks, his team lacked a complete picture of the business.

With Campfire, all four entities now run through a single general ledger. Every Stripe and Brex transaction flows in automatically, and revenue recognition is in the system for the first time - giving the team financial statements that actually reflect reality. 

It also shaved five to six days off their monthly close.

What their team is most excited about goes beyond the close. PostHog has a value called "making public", which means controlled democratization of data. With granular permissions in Campfire, their CEO and select team leads can now access and query financial performance using Ember without ever having to make a request to finance.

Watching PostHog scale at this pace, and being the system they trust to scale with them, means a lot.

Huge congrats to Fraser and the entire PostHog team. We love working with you. 🔥

posts.content:
At Q2 planning we made a commitment that everybody on the team should primarily be using AI to enable themselves to be AI-native. 

We've now made a hiring shift to prioritise AI-native over experience. Experience is now a tiebreaker, not the gate. 

here's what we mean:

→ ai-native isn't "experienced + a chatgpt subscription." it's a different version of the job. 
→ the ai-native finance manager has the close on a schedule. the traditional one is still proof-reading the management report on day 30. 
→ the ai-native talent partner runs analysis on what makes posthog hires succeed. (it turns out fast talkers do well here.) 
→ the ai-native ops manager has automated offer letters and contracts across 30+ countries. 
→ years of experience still matter — as a tiebreaker, not as a moat. 
→ "ai-curious" and "ai-native" are not the same thing. screen for workflows and artefacts, not chatgpt subscriptions.

The practical result: our hiring plan for the next 2-3 years is smaller than it would have been a year ago. each ai-native hire is leveraged enough that we need fewer of them.
